# Version control with `git`

This section will be on the homework but I won't put it on the exams.

## Introduction

The setup guide explains the `git add` - `git commit` - `git push` idiom to hand in your labs. In this unit we look at what those commands actually do, and at the handful of other commands that you will likely use if you pursue data science / engineering.

`git` keeps a complete history of a folder of files (hence why it's great for teams working on text files housing code, i.e., for "version control"). Every saved snapshot is called a **commit**; it has an author, a date, a message, and a short identifying alphanumeric code e.g., `a1b2c3d`. Nothing in a commit is ever silently overwritten, which is why `git` is such a good safety net.

`git` is not the only version control system, but it is the dominant one by far. Nobody counts "worldwide users" of a free tool exactly, so the best we have is the share of developers who say they use each one in surveys (people can name several, so shares can add to more than 100%).

+------------------+------+-------------+-------------------------+---------------------------+

|                  |      |             | (approx.)               |                           |
+:=================+=====:+:============+========================:+:==========================+
| `git`            | 2005 | distributed | ~94%                    | Almost everything,        |
|                  |      |             |                         | including `git` itself    |
+------------------+------+-------------+-------------------------+---------------------------+
| Subversion (SVN) | 2000 | centralized | ~5%                     | Older companies and some  |
|                  |      |             |                         | academic groups           |
+------------------+------+-------------+-------------------------+---------------------------+
| Perforce         | 1995 | centralized | a few % (no clean data) | Game studios, huge binary |
|                  |      |             |                         | assets                    |
+------------------+------+-------------+-------------------------+---------------------------+
| Mercurial (`hg`) | 2005 | distributed | ~1%                     | Legacy projects (Mozilla  |
|                  |      |             |                         | moved to git)             |
+------------------+------+-------------+-------------------------+---------------------------+
| CVS              | 1990 | centralized | ~0% (legacy projects    | Museum piece; SVN was     |
|                  |      |             | only)                   | built to replace it       |
+------------------+------+-------------+-------------------------+---------------------------+

: Version control systems, ordered by share of developers. Survey figures are approximate and the 2025 numbers are secondhand (via [RhodeCode's summary](https://rhodecode.com/insights) of the Stack Overflow survey); Perforce and CVS have no reliable current figure, so their order is a rough judgement from [a Gartner legacy-project poll](https://www.gartner.com/peer-community/poll/what-version-control-system-vcs-are-you-using-for-legacy-projects).

`git` is the tool; GitHub is a website/company (owned by Microsoft) that hosts `git` repositories (which are called the "remotes" and are usually named `origin`, `master`, `main`). GitHub also manages "pull requests", issue tracking and so on. Here is a list of places where `git` is served:

+----------------------+-----------+--------------------+--------------------------------------+

+:=====================+:==========+===================:+:=====================================+

+----------------------+-----------+--------------------+--------------------------------------+

+----------------------+-----------+--------------------+--------------------------------------+

|                      |           |                    | companies                            |
+----------------------+-----------+--------------------+--------------------------------------+

|                      |           |                    | Mercurial support                    |
+----------------------+-----------+--------------------+--------------------------------------+
| Azure DevOps, others | various   | no public figure   | Common in Microsoft shops,           |
|                      |           |                    | SourceForge is the old-timer         |
+----------------------+-----------+--------------------+--------------------------------------+

: Git hosting services, ordered by accounts. GitHub's figure is from its 2025 Octoverse report (via [secondary coverage](https://www.getpanto.ai/blog/github-statistics)); Bitbucket's is Atlassian's 2025 "developers" count; GitLab's is an undated third-party estimate. Accounts are not active users, and one person may hold several. The self-hosted row is my own order-of-magnitude guess, not a measurement: no one publishes a total, so it assumes a large share of GitLab's accounts and most of Bitbucket's enterprise users sit on company-run servers. Private repos kept on GitHub itself are not counted. 

GitHub is the biggest venue for open source software in the world. Most of the projects we met in the previous section keep their code there: [Python](https://github.com/python/cpython), [R](https://github.com/wch/r-source) (a mirror, see below), [Linux](https://github.com/torvalds/linux) (also a mirror), [`pandas`](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas), [`NumPy`](https://github.com/numpy/numpy), [`TensorFlow`](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow), [`PyTorch`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch), [`Kubernetes`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes), [`VS Code`](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode) and [Quarto](https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli), [`git`](https://github.com/git/git) itself, along with millions of smaller libraries. Even projects that develop elsewhere keep a mirror on GitHub, such as the Linux kernel (developed through mailing lists), R (developed in Subversion) and [PostgreSQL](https://github.com/postgres/postgres) (which runs its own git server), because that is where people look for code. It became the default for three reasons:

* **Network effect:** with about 180 million developers, a project on GitHub is where its potential users and contributors already are.
* **Low friction:** anyone can **fork** (copy) a project, change it and propose the change back with a **pull request**, with no permission needed. Issues, discussion and automated testing live on the same page.
* **Visibility:** search, **stars** and your commit history on your profile make GitHub a public CV, and employers often look at it. In a 2017 [HackerRank survey](https://www.hackerrank.com/research/developer-skills/2018), most hiring managers said they look for proven skill such as previous work and projects/GitHub, and in interviews with employers ([Marlow and Dabbish, 2013](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/262248832_Activity_traces_and_signals_in_software_developer_recruitment_and_hiring)) they said they trust visible activity more than résumé claims. Microsoft bought GitHub in 2018 for about $7.5 billion likely because they wanted to buy the network of all the developers.

That is also why you hand in your labs through it: the habits you build in this course (commit, push, pull request) are the ones used by open source projects everywhere and companies everywhere. You are learning the standard for any sort of software engineering and data science.

## Demo rules
I'll run every command below in the actual 52002 course repository. The first demo, a live commit and push of this very lecture file, is real. Everything after it happens only on **throw-away "branches"** that we delete at the end, so `main` is never touched by it (`main` is the production code for that runs this course) Two rules for the throw-away part that I'll stick to: never `git push` those branches, and use explicit file names with `git add` (not `git commit -a`), because our working folder may hold other unfinished changes.

## The places a change travels through

A change to a file passes through several places on its way to GitHub:

```
 working folder     staging area      local repository   GitHub (the mothership - for sharing with others)
  (your files)      (next commit)      (your history)     (remote: origin)
        |                 |                   |                   |
        |---- git add ---->                   |                   |
        |                 |--- git commit ---->                   |
        |                 |                   |---- git push ----->
        |                 |                   |                   |
        <----------------------- git pull ------------------------|
```

Each level is confusing. The *staging area* lets you choose exactly which changes go into the next commit: `add` puts changes into the staging area, `commit` saves what is staged as one snapshot. And `git status` tells you what is where. Finally, `push` sends it to the mothership.

## The everyday loop

**Live demo: commit and push this lecture.** Let's save the file you are reading to GitHub. Add a blank line at the end of the lecture file (any whitespace will do). First we take a look at what is gitignored.

```bash
#do not run the commands in this chunk on your machine --- this is for me, the owner of the course repo only
cd ~/workspace/HUJI_52002_Fall_2026
```

Now we walk through the add-commit-push path. 

```bash
git status                          # which branch am I on (we'll discuss this soon)? what has changed in this branch?
#I'm going to make an edit in this file (delete a word, add a word, add a blank line)
git status
git diff --stat                        # which files changed, how, and by how many lines
git diff --ignore-blank-lines --stat   # git can also ignore blank lines: our line no longer counts
git diff                               #see the diff itself (additions are colored green and subtractions are colored red)
git add lectures/lec03_git_parquet_databases.qmd   # stage just that file ("git add ."" means stage all files that were edited)
git diff                               #clean as diff measures difference between
git diff --staged                      # but the change is in the staging area: this is what the next commit would contain
git restore --staged lectures/lec03_git_parquet_databases.qmd   # undo the staging (old spelling: git reset lectures/lec03_git_parquet_databases.qmd); our edit stays in the file
git status                             # "Changes not staged for commit" again
git diff                               # and the change is back in the diff
git add lectures/lec03_git_parquet_databases.qmd   # stage it again, to go on

git commit -m "lec03: small changes and whitespace, live git demo"
git push                            # upload; now refresh the file's page on GitHub
git log --oneline -n 3              # our commit is on top
#the top line should be
#<commit code> (HEAD -> main, origin/main, origin/HEAD) lec03: whitespace, live git demo 
#now I'll open https://github.com/kapelner/HUJI_52002_Fall_2026 and click on "commits" and look at the diff
```

What do these things mean?

HEAD: the current branch, and through it the current commit
main            your local branch (moves when you commit)
origin/main and origin/HEAD we'll discuss later if we have time

Each commit contains all files compressed at that specific point in history (if the file doesn't change between commits, it just points to a previous commit so it's not actually wasteful). This makes it very fast to "checkout" code at any point. But this is the reason saving large files that constantly change is NOT a good idea. This is why large files should be gitignored!

You can design the system to just save the diffs each time and then replay the diffs at every point in history (CVS, SVN) but git chooses to be faster for checkout.


A couple conveniences I use constantly:

* `git add .` stages *everything* in the folder that is not ignored. Run `git status` first. If you don't check the status, then you make mistakes e.g. a 35 MB `covid.csv` ends up in a repository by accident.
* `git commit -am "msg"` does `git add <all staged>` then commits with a message stages every change to files git **already tracks**, but it skips **new** files. That is why the setup guide runs `git add .` first: it stages new files too.
* Write commit messages that say *what and why* ("fix off-by-one in header skip"), not "stuff" or "asdf". You will need to read them in six months from now and you won't remember what you did. Also, if you work with other people, they will need to read them immediately.

Remember: once you hit `git push`, it sends your new commits to GitHub, the mothership for your code that is indelibly recorded forever (see [my github page](https://github.com/kapelner) and click "arctic") that your teammates can access.

What will likely not be useful `git` commands for you in this class:

* `git pull` brings other people's (or your other computer's) commits down. Pull before you start working, and push when you are done. Since nobody else is pushing to your repo, there is nothing ever to pull!
* Set your working directory to your main worksapce folder then `git init <new repo_name>` creates a new repo on your local machine. Useful for you own tracking. There's no mothership unless you connect it to one. `git` can work without a mothership. But if Zohar's cat eats your computer... Also, don't run `git init` inside a folder that is already inside another repo, because that creates a repo within a repo. That's a huge mess... To connect your local repo to the mothership, make a new repo on the mothership then use `git remote add origin <url>`.


## What is a branch?

A **branch** is a separate line of development. You can think of it as a parallel copy of the project in which you can edit, commit and break things without affecting anyone else's copy. If the experiment works, you **merge** it back; if it doesn't, you delete the branch and nothing is lost.

Under the hood a branch is not a copy at all. It is just a **movable label that points to one commit** (a tiny file with a commit code in it), so creating a branch is instant and costs nothing, even for a huge project. When you commit, the label of the branch you are on moves forward to the new commit. `HEAD` (the "where am I?" pointer from before) says which branch is the current one:

```
                 C---D         <- lec03-demo   (a branch we are experimenting on)
                /
        A---B---E---F          <- main         (the production code, untouched)
                    ^
                   HEAD  (if we are standing on main)
```

Here the two lines share the history A--B and then go their own ways: `main` kept going with E and F, and `lec03-demo` has its own commits C and D. Nothing that happens on one line shows up on the other until we merge.

Why use them?

* **Safety:** `main` always holds working code (in this course, the code that builds the website and the labs). Experiments happen elsewhere.
* **Parallel work:** several people (or you, on two ideas) work at the same time without stepping on each other. This is how teams of thousands of developers share one repository.
* **Review:** a branch is what you hand to a colleague in a pull request for review before it is merged into `main`.

The few commands we need:

```bash
git branch                    # list the branches; * marks the current one
git switch -c new-name        # create a branch and move onto it (-c = create)
git switch main               # move back to an existing branch (your files change to match it!)
git branch -d new-name        # delete a merged branch (-D forces it if it still has unmerged commits)
```

Now we can play with the undo commands safely.

**Live demo: three ways to undo.** We play on a throw-away branch so `main` is never touched. First, make a good commit and then a bad one:

```bash
git switch -c undo-demo                    # throw-away branch to play on
echo "good line" > notes.txt
git add notes.txt
git commit -m "add notes"
echo "BAD line" >> notes.txt
git commit -am "oops: a bad line"
git log --oneline -n 3                     # the bad commit is on top
```



**Going back in time.** Because every commit is a complete snapshot, it's easy to "go back in time" if you feel like you messed something up. Going back one step just means pointing git at the commit below ours in `git log`. We first check to ensure this is where we want to rewind to:

```bash
git log --oneline -n 3
git show --stat HEAD~1          # "one commit before HEAD" (HEAD~2 is two before, and so on)
```

If you want to check an arbitrary point in the past, you can use the commit code:

```bash
git log --oneline -n 10
git show --stat a23dd65   # or just paste the code of that commit from git log --oneline
```

`git show` only *looks*. To put the whole working folder back to that point:

```bash
wc -l lectures/lec03_git_parquet_databases.qmd     # the number of lines now
git switch --detach HEAD~1      # rewind the working folder one step; main does not move
wc -l lectures/lec03_git_parquet_databases.qmd     # one line fewer: our blank line is gone
git status                      # "HEAD detached at <code>"
git log --oneline main -n 3     # main still points at the newest commit
git switch main                 # come back to the present (git switch - also works)
wc -l lectures/lec03_git_parquet_databases.qmd     # the blank line is back
```

These all go back one step in the same way: `git switch --detach HEAD~1`, `git switch --detach HEAD^`, `git switch --detach <commit code>`, and the old spelling `git checkout HEAD~1` (see `checkout` below). To see just one file as it was, without moving anything, use `git show HEAD~1:lectures/lec03_git_parquet_databases.qmd`.

After `git switch --detach`, `HEAD` points straight at a commit instead of at a branch (a **detached HEAD**), as if you were visiting the old snapshot. It is safe for looking around, since `main` has not moved. Don't commit while detached: a commit made there belongs to no branch and is easy to lose. If you want to start work from the old snapshot, give it a branch first with `git switch -c new-branch-name`.

"Visiting" is not undoing. Here are the three types of "undos":

* To undo a commit by adding a *new* commit that undoes the previous commit, use `git revert`. History is only added to, so this is the safe choice for pushed commits. Reverting D gives a new commit D' where D' undoes D to get back to C (to get back to B, revert twice, etc):

  ```
  A->B->C->D   --git revert D-->   A->B->C->D->D'
  ```

* To move the branch back, use `git reset --mixed` or `git reset --hard`. C and D will no longer be on the branch so you are destroying the work in C and D

  ```
  A->B->C->D   --git reset --mixed B-->   A->B   (files still contain C's and D's changes, un-staged)
  A->B->C->D   --git reset --hard B-->    A->B   (any work in C and D is destroyed permanently)
  ```

* To bring back just one file, use `git restore`. It changes your working folder, not the commit history:

  ```
  A->B->C->D   --git restore file-->   A->B->C->D   (only the file in the working folder changes)
  ```

I can demo these different types of "undo" but I don't want to mess up the course repo! So we take a slight detour now to talk about branches first.


`git revert` undoes a commit by making a **new** commit that does the opposite. History is only added to, never rewritten, so it is the safe choice for anything you have already pushed:

```bash
git revert --no-edit HEAD                  # new commit "Revert 'oops: a bad line'"
git log --oneline -n 4                     # the bad commit is still there, followed by its undo
cat notes.txt                              # the BAD line is gone
```

`git restore` fixes **files**, not history. It never moves the branch:

```bash
echo "scribble" >> notes.txt
git restore notes.txt                      # throw away uncommitted edits: the file is back to the last commit (cannot be undone!)
git restore --source=HEAD~1 notes.txt      # copy the file as it was one commit ago (the BAD version) into the working folder
git status                                 # modified, not committed: we are still on the same commit
git restore notes.txt                      # and discard that too
```

`git reset` **moves the branch** back to an earlier commit and, depending on the option, what happens to your edits. Let's drop the revert commit and then the bad commit:

```bash
git reset --hard HEAD~1                    # branch moves back one commit; the working folder is made to match (the revert commit is gone)
git log --oneline -n 3                     # the bad commit is on top again
git reset --soft HEAD~1                    # branch moves back, but the change stays STAGED
git status                                 # "Changes to be committed": notes.txt still has the BAD line
git reset                                  # un-stage it (--mixed is the default): the change stays in the file, but not staged
git status                                 # "Changes not staged for commit"
git reset --hard                           # now throw the change away: the file is back to the last commit
cat notes.txt                              # just the good line
```

+----------------------+-----------+-----------+---------------------------+
| `git reset` option   | moves the | un-stages | changes your files        |
|                      | branch    |           |                           |
+:=====================+:=========:+:=========:+:==========================+
| `--soft`             | yes       | no        | no                        |
+----------------------+-----------+-----------+---------------------------+
| `--mixed` (default)  | yes       | yes       | no                        |
+----------------------+-----------+-----------+---------------------------+
| `--hard`             | yes       | yes       | **yes** (destroys         |
|                      |           |           | uncommitted work)         |
+----------------------+-----------+-----------+---------------------------+

Because `reset` rewrites history, don't use it on commits you have already pushed (use `revert` for those). If you reset too far, `git reflog` lists where HEAD has been, and `git reset --hard <code>` returns there. Clean up the playground:

```bash
git switch main
git branch -D undo-demo                    # delete the throw-away branch (-D because it was never merged)
```

Now let's talk about a powerful.


```bash
git switch -c lec03-demo        # switch to a new, throw-away branch called lec03-demo to play on (more on branches below)
echo "first line" > demo_notes.txt  #make a new file
git status                      # demo_notes.txt is "untracked": git sees it but does not track it
git add demo_notes.txt          # stage it
git status                      # now "to be committed"
git commit -m "add demo notes"  # save the snapshot
git log --oneline               # the history, one line per commit
```

Edit the file and look at what changed before you commit it:

```bash
echo "second line" >> demo_notes.txt
git diff                        # unstaged changes: working folder vs. the last add
git add demo_notes.txt
git diff --staged               # staged changes: what the next commit will contain
git commit -m "extend demo notes"
```


Looking back at the history:

```bash
git log --oneline --graph       # compact history; --graph draws the branches
git log -p demo_notes.txt       # every change ever made to one file
git show HEAD                   # the last commit in full (HEAD means "where I am now")
git show HEAD~1                 # the commit before it
git blame demo_notes.txt        # who wrote each line, and in which commit
```

## What git should not hold: `.gitignore`

Git is made for code and small text files. It is **not** made for big data: every version of a file is stored forever, and GitHub rejects any single file over 100 MB. Data, results and scratch files are kept out of the repository with a plain-text file called `.gitignore`, which lives in the repository (so it is versioned and shared like any other file). Each line is a pattern for files git should pretend not to see. Our own repo already has one:

```bash
cat .gitignore                  # includes the scratch/ line you added in Lab 1
git status --ignored            # also list what is being ignored
git check-ignore -v scratch/lec03/covid.csv   # WHICH rule ignores this file? (prints the file and line)
```

The pattern rules are short:

+----------------------+-----------------------------------------------+
| Line in `.gitignore` | Meaning                                       |
+:=====================+:==============================================+
| `# comment`          | a comment; blank lines are skipped            |
+----------------------+-----------------------------------------------+
| `*.csv`              | any file ending in `.csv`, in any folder      |
|                      | (`*` matches any characters, but not `/`)     |
+----------------------+-----------------------------------------------+
| `scratch/`           | a folder (the trailing `/`) and everything    |
|                      | inside it, wherever it is                     |
+----------------------+-----------------------------------------------+
| `/data.csv`          | only `data.csv` in the top folder of the repo |
|                      | (a leading `/` anchors the pattern)           |
+----------------------+-----------------------------------------------+
| `**/old/`            | a folder called `old` at any depth            |
+----------------------+-----------------------------------------------+
| `!keep.csv`          | an **exception**: do not ignore `keep.csv`,   |
|                      | even if an earlier line ignored it            |
+----------------------+-----------------------------------------------+

The last rule is read top to bottom and the last matching line wins, so put exceptions after the pattern they relax:

```bash
printf '*.log\n*.gz\n!important.log\n' >> .gitignore
touch a.log important.log data.csv.gz
git status -s                   # only important.log shows up as untracked
git check-ignore -v a.log       # shows the rule: .gitignore:NN:*.log
git add .gitignore && git commit -m "ignore logs and gz files"
rm a.log important.log data.csv.gz
```

Three things trip people up:

* **Ignoring does not untrack.** `.gitignore` only affects files git is *not yet* tracking. If you already committed `covid.csv`, adding it to `.gitignore` changes nothing. Tell git to stop tracking it, and leave the file on disk:

```bash
echo "big data" > big.csv
git add big.csv                 # oops: a data file gets added...
git commit -m "oops, committed data"
echo "big.csv" >> .gitignore    # ...adding it to .gitignore now does nothing: git already tracks it
git rm --cached big.csv         # stop tracking; the file stays in the folder
git add .gitignore && git commit -m "stop tracking big.csv"
rm big.csv                      # (demo only) delete the leftover file
git status
 ```

The file is still in the *old* commits. Removing a big file from the history is a harder job (a tool such as `git filter-repo`), so it is much better to check `git status` before every commit.
* **Ignore rules are per repository.** Junk that belongs to *your* machine and editor (`.DS_Store`, `*.swp`, `.vscode/`) can go in a personal global file instead of every project's `.gitignore`: `git config --global core.excludesFile ~/.gitignore_global`.
* **Empty folders are not tracked.** Git tracks files, not folders. The usual trick to keep an empty folder is a placeholder file inside it, e.g. `data/.gitkeep`, plus the lines `data/*` and `!data/.gitkeep` in `.gitignore`.

## Undoing things, place by place

Which undo you want depends on how far the mistake has travelled. Look at the picture of the places again, find where the mistake is now, and use the matching tool:

+-------------------------+-----------------------------+------------------------------+
| The mistake is in...    | Use                         | Is it safe?                  |
+:========================+:============================+:=============================+
| the working folder      | `git restore file`          | **loses** the edits for good |
| (edited, not added)     |                             |                              |
+-------------------------+-----------------------------+------------------------------+
| the staging area        | `git restore --staged file` | safe, nothing is lost        |
| (added, not committed)  |                             |                              |
+-------------------------+-----------------------------+------------------------------+
| the local repository    | `git reset`,                | safe for you alone; commits  |
| (committed, not pushed) | `git commit --amend`        | can be recovered with        |
|                         |                             | `git reflog`                 |
+-------------------------+-----------------------------+------------------------------+
| the remote (pushed)     | `git revert`, then          | safe for everybody           |
|                         | `git push`                  |                              |
+-------------------------+-----------------------------+------------------------------+

### Out of the staging area

You ran `git add` on something you did not mean to, say a big data file. Unstage it. The file stays in your folder; git just stops planning to commit it:

```bash
echo "oops" > big.csv
git add big.csv                     # whoops
git status                          # "Changes to be committed: new file: big.csv"
git restore --staged big.csv        # out of the staging area; big.csv is still in the folder
git status                          # big.csv is "untracked" again
rm big.csv                          # (demo only)
```

`git restore --staged .` unstages everything at once. For a file that git already tracks, `--staged` keeps your edits in the folder and only removes them from the next commit, which is also how you split one pile of edits into two commits. (You will see the older spelling `git reset HEAD file` in tutorials; it does the same thing.) Do not confuse this with plain `git restore file`, which throws the *edits* away.

### Out of the local repository

You already ran `git commit`, but have not pushed. Nobody else has seen it, so you are free to rewrite it:

```bash
# the last commit has the wrong message, or you forgot a file:
git add forgotten.txt
git commit --amend -m "better message"      # replaces the last commit with a corrected one

# the last commit should not exist at all:
echo "oops" > big.csv
git add big.csv && git commit -m "add big.csv by mistake"
git reset --soft HEAD~1             # undo the commit, but leave the changes STAGED
git reset HEAD~1                    # undo the commit, and leave the changes in the folder, unstaged
git reset --hard HEAD~1             # undo the commit AND delete the changes (dangerous)
```

`HEAD~1` means "one commit before where I am"; `HEAD~3` goes back three. The three flavors of `git reset` differ only in how far back the changes are taken: `--soft` moves only the branch, the default (`--mixed`) also empties the staging area, and `--hard` also overwrites the working folder.

A very common case in this course is a big file that was committed by accident but not yet pushed. Remove it from the commit itself, so that it never exists in the history that you push:

```bash
git rm --cached big.csv             # take it out of git's tracking, but keep the file on disk
git commit --amend --no-edit        # rewrite the last commit without it, keeping the message
```

(If it was buried a few commits back, `git reset --soft HEAD~3` uncommits the last three, you unstage the file, and you commit again.)

**Safety net: `git reflog`.** Even after `reset --hard`, committed work is almost never gone. Git keeps a private log of everywhere `HEAD` has been, for about three months:

```bash
git reset --hard HEAD~1             # oops, that threw away a commit we wanted
git reflog                          # newest first; HEAD@{1} is where we were before the reset
git reset --hard HEAD@{1}           # go back
```

This rescues *commits*. It cannot rescue edits that you never added or committed (`git restore file` and `reset --hard` really do lose those), which is why committing early and often, or `git stash`, is cheap insurance.

### Out of the remote (`origin`)

You already ran `git push`. Other people (and your other computers) may have pulled these commits, so rewriting them now would give everybody conflicting histories. The standard, safe undo is a **new commit that cancels the old one**:

```bash
git log --oneline -n 3              # find the id of the bad commit
git revert a1b2c3d                  # new commit that undoes commit a1b2c3d (git opens an editor; save and close)
git push                            # the history only grows, so a plain push works
git revert HEAD                     # shortcut: undo the very last commit
```

If you are the **only** person using that branch (say, your own homework branch) you can rewrite the history instead, and then overwrite the remote with a *force* push:

```bash
git reset --hard HEAD~1             # remove the last commit locally
git push --force-with-lease         # overwrite origin; refuses if somebody pushed in the meantime
```

Use `--force-with-lease`, not plain `--force`: it only overwrites what you last saw, so you cannot silently destroy a colleague's commit. Anyone else who already has the old commits must repair their copy, and shared branches such as `main` are often protected against force pushes, so this is the exception.

Two special cases:

* **A branch on origin you want gone:** `git push origin --delete lec03-demo` (your local copy of the branch is separate: `git branch -D`).
* **A secret or a huge file was pushed.** Deleting it in a later commit does not help; it stays in the history, and anybody can check out the old commit. A pushed password, token or key must be treated as **public**: change it at once, and only then clean the history (with a tool such as `git filter-repo` plus a force push). For a file over 100 MB, GitHub refuses the push, but the bad commit still exists in your *local* repository: fix it locally as above (`reset --soft`, or `rm --cached` plus `--amend`), and push again.

We will not run the remote commands live in the demo, since we never push the demo branches.

## `checkout`: moving around

`git checkout` is the old Swiss-army knife of git. It does several unrelated jobs depending on what you give it:

```bash
git checkout lec03-demo             # switch to the branch lec03-demo
git checkout -b lec03-exp           # create the branch lec03-exp and switch to it
git checkout a1b2c3d                # look at the folder as it was at an old commit
git checkout -- demo_notes.txt      # throw away uncommitted edits in demo_notes.txt
```

Because that is confusing, since git 2.23 the jobs were split into two clearer commands: `git switch` (for branches: `git switch lec03-demo`, `git switch -c lec03-exp`) and `git restore` (for files, as above). Both spellings work, and you will see `checkout` in most tutorials and answers online, so you need to read both.

Checking out an old commit puts you in a "detached HEAD" state: you are looking at the past, and anything you commit there belongs to no branch. Look around, and then go back with `git switch -` (back to where you were) or `git switch lec03-demo`.

## Branches and merging

A **branch** is a separate line of commits. It lets you try something (a new analysis, a risky rewrite) without touching the main line, and join it back when it works. (For the demo, `lec03-demo` plays the role of `main`.)

```bash
git branch                          # list branches (the current one has a *)
git branch --show-current           # just the name of the branch you are on
git switch -c lec03-exp             # new branch, and move onto it
                                    # (= `git branch lec03-exp` to create it, then `git switch lec03-exp`)
echo "an idea" >> demo_notes.txt
git commit -m "try an idea" demo_notes.txt
git switch lec03-demo               # back: demo_notes.txt no longer has the idea!
git merge lec03-exp                 # bring the experiment's commits in
git branch -d lec03-exp             # delete a branch you are done with
```

`git branch` *manages* branches (list, create, rename with `git branch -m new-name`, delete); `git switch` *moves* between them. `git branch -a` also lists the branches that exist on GitHub.

When two branches changed the *same lines*, git cannot choose and reports a **merge conflict**. Make one on purpose:

```bash
git switch -c lec03-fix
echo "from fix" > conflict.txt
git add conflict.txt && git commit -m "fix: add conflict.txt"
git switch lec03-demo
echo "from demo" > conflict.txt
git add conflict.txt && git commit -m "demo: add conflict.txt"
git merge lec03-fix                 # CONFLICT (add/add) in conflict.txt
git status                          # "both added: conflict.txt"
cat conflict.txt
```

git marks the file for you:

```
<<<<<<< HEAD
from demo
=======
from fix
>>>>>>> lec03-fix
```

Everything between `<<<<<<<` and `=======` is your side, and the rest up to `>>>>>>>` is the other branch's side. To resolve it, edit the file into what you want (and delete the three marker lines), then finish the merge:

```bash
echo "resolved" > conflict.txt      # or edit it by hand
git add conflict.txt
git commit                          # git suggests a merge message; save and close the editor
```

If you panic in the middle of a merge, `git merge --abort` puts everything back as it was before.

## `stash`: put your work aside

You are in the middle of an edit, and you need to switch branches or pull, but git refuses because of your uncommitted changes. You do not want to commit half-finished work. `git stash` puts **all** your uncommitted changes (in our repo that includes the lecture file we are editing!) in a drawer and gives you back a clean folder:

```bash
echo "half-finished thought" >> demo_notes.txt
git stash                           # shelve the changes; the folder is clean again
git status                          # nothing to commit
git switch lec03-fix                # switching is easy now
git switch lec03-demo
git stash list                      # what is in the drawer
git stash pop                       # take the newest stash out and re-apply it
git restore demo_notes.txt          # drop the half-finished thought; we only needed it for the demo
```

Useful variants: `git stash -u` also shelves *new* (untracked) files, which a plain `stash` leaves behind; `git stash push -m "wip: header fix" file1` shelves only `file1` and labels the stash; `git stash apply` re-applies but keeps the stash in the drawer; `git stash drop` throws a stash away.

## `worktree`: a second folder, same repository

`stash` is for a quick interruption. For a longer one (a hotfix while your analysis is half-done, or comparing two versions of a script side by side) a **worktree** is cleaner: a second folder, with its own branch checked out, that shares the same history as your main folder. Nothing in your main folder is disturbed.

+------------+------------------------+----------------------------+------------------+
| Tool       | What it holds          | Lifetime                   | Shared with      |
|            |                        |                            | GitHub?          |
+:===========+:=======================+:===========================+:=================+
| `stash`    | Uncommitted edits, put | Temporary: meant to be     | Never            |
|            | in a drawer            | popped within minutes or   |                  |
|            |                        | hours                      |                  |
+------------+------------------------+----------------------------+------------------+
| `worktree` | A second folder with a | As long as the folder      | Only through its |
|            | branch checked out     | exists; remove it when     | branch           |
|            |                        | done                       |                  |
+------------+------------------------+----------------------------+------------------+
| `branch`   | A line of commits      | Permanent until you delete | Yes, if you push |
|            |                        | it                         | it               |
+------------+------------------------+----------------------------+------------------+

: Three ways to set work aside. A worktree is a place to work and needs a branch; a stash is not a commit on any branch.

A rule of thumb:

- **Stash:** "I'll be back in five minutes."
- **Worktree:** "I need a second workspace while this one stays as it is."
- **Branch:** "This is a real line of work I'll keep and merge."

```bash
git worktree add ../lec03-wt -b lec03-wt    # new folder next to the repo, on a new branch
git worktree list                           # every folder attached to this repo
cd ../lec03-wt                              # work, commit and run things here as usual
cd -                                        # back to the main folder: its files never changed
git worktree remove ../lec03-wt             # done: delete the folder (--force if it has changes)
git branch -D lec03-wt                      # the branch is separate; delete it too
```

It is far cheaper than a second `git clone`, since the history is stored only once. Two rules: a branch can be checked out in only one worktree at a time, and always remove a worktree with `git worktree remove` (if you just delete the folder, `git worktree prune` clears the leftover record). Tools like Claude Code use throw-away worktrees to try changes without touching your files.

## Working with GitHub

```bash
git clone https://github.com/<user>/<repo>.git   # copy a repository (history included) to your computer
git remote -v                       # where is "origin"?
git fetch                           # download new commits but do not change your files
git pull                            # fetch + merge into your current branch
git push                            # upload your commits
```

If `git push` is rejected with "failed to push some refs" or "Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do not have", somebody (maybe you, from another computer) pushed first. Run `git pull`, fix any conflicts as above, and push again.

## Clean up the demo

```bash
git stash list                      # should be empty (or only stashes that are really yours)
git switch main                     # back to the real branch
git worktree list                   # should show only the main folder
git branch -D lec03-demo lec03-fix  # -D : delete even though these were never merged into main
rm -f demo_notes.txt conflict.txt big.csv   # leftovers, if any (normally there are none)
git status                          # back to exactly where we started
```

The demo commits disappear with the branches, so nothing from the demo ever reaches GitHub.

## Cheat sheet

+-------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------+
| I want to...                              | Command                                     |
+===========================================+=============================================+
| see what changed                          | `git status`, `git diff`                    |
+-------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------+
| save my work                              | `git add .` then `git commit -m "msg"`      |
+-------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------+
| share it                                  | `git push`                                  |
+-------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------+
| get others' work                          | `git pull`                                  |
+-------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------+
| see the history                           | `git log --oneline --graph`                 |
+-------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------+
| discard edits to a file                   | `git restore file`                          |
+-------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------+
| un-stage a file                           | `git restore --staged file`                 |
+-------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------+
| undo a pushed commit                      | `git revert <id>`                           |
+-------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------+
| try something on the side                 | `git switch -c name`, then `git merge name` |
+-------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------+
| set unfinished work aside                 | `git stash`, later `git stash pop`          |
+-------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------+
| work on another branch in a second folder | `git worktree add ../name -b name`, later   |
|                                           | `git worktree remove ../name`               |
+-------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------+
| see which branch I am on                  | `git branch --show-current`                 |
+-------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------+
| keep a file out of git                    | add it to `.gitignore`                      |
+-------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------+
| stop tracking a big file                  | `git rm --cached file` and add it to        |
|                                           | `.gitignore`                                |
+-------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------+
| find out why a file is ignored            | `git check-ignore -v file`                  |
+-------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------+

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it
(1) On a new branch, change `demo_notes.txt` and commit. (2) Switch to another branch, make an uncommitted edit to the same file, and try to switch back or merge. What does git say? Use `git stash` to get out of it, and then `git stash pop`. (3) Which of `restore`, `revert` and `reset` would you use for a mistake that is only in your working folder, for one that you committed but did not push, and for one that you already pushed? (4) Add `*.tmp` to `.gitignore`, create `x.tmp`, and use `git check-ignore -v x.tmp` to see which line ignores it. Then clean up the demo.
:::


# Tabular data and its types

Everything so far in this course focused on the CSV: plain text, one row per line. Before we look for a better file format, we should say precisely what kind of data a CSV holds, because the kind of data decides what a good format for it looks like. This unit defines **tabular data** (rows and columns) and the **types** of the values in a column. The next unit uses both words to motivate a new file format.

Make a scratch folder for this lecture and bring the data along (we use it again in the database unit):

```bash
mkdir -p ~/workspace/HUJI_52002_Fall_2026/scratch/lec03
cd ~/workspace/HUJI_52002_Fall_2026/scratch/lec03
cp ../lec01/covid.csv .
```

## What is tabular data?

A CSV holds **tabular data**, so let us define it. A table is a rectangle with two directions:

* Each **row** is one **object** (also called a subject, an observation, a case, a record, a unit, an example or an instance): one thing that we measured.
* Each **column** is one **attribute** (also called a feature, a characteristic, a variable, a field or a predictor): one property that we measured, for every object.

Usually the # of rows is denoted $n$ and the number of columns denoted $p$.

Every row has the same columns, and every column holds one kind of value (all dates, or all integers, or all text). Here are the first rows of `covid.csv`:

```bash
head -n 4 covid.csv | column -s, -t
```

```
date        county     state       fips   cases  deaths
2020-01-21  Snohomish  Washington  53061  1      0
2020-01-22  Snohomish  Washington  53061  1      0
2020-01-23  Snohomish  Washington  53061  1      0
```

The six columns are the attributes. Each row is one object, and here the *object* is the **report for one county on one day**: "Snohomish County on 2020-01-21". It is *not* a county, since Snohomish appears in many rows (`date`, `county` and `state` together identify a row, because many states have a Washington County), and deciding what one row stands for is the first question to ask of any dataset. In this context, the vocabulary I would use is "this file has 884,737 records and 6 fields per record".

Different communities use different words for the same two ideas:

+------------------+------------------------+------------------------------------------+
|                  | Rows                   | Columns                                  |
+:=================+:=======================+:=========================================+
| Statistics       | subjects, observations | variables                                |
+------------------+------------------------+------------------------------------------+
| Machine learning | examples, instances    | features (the $X$s), the label (the $y$) |
+------------------+------------------------+------------------------------------------+
| Databases        | records, tuples        | fields, attributes                       |
+------------------+------------------------+------------------------------------------+
| R / Python       | rows of a data frame   | columns of a data frame                  |
+------------------+------------------------+------------------------------------------+

: The same rectangle, in four vocabularies. You will see all of them in this course.

Not all data is tabular. A nested JSON record (e.g., `{"name": "Kapelner", "address": {"city": "London"}, "langs": ["R", "Python"]}`, which has a record inside a record and a list inside a record), an image, or a paragraph of text is not a rectangle of objects by attributes. But for now, we will be focusing on tables.

## Data types (= column types)

Every column has a **type**: the kind of thing its values are, which decides what you are allowed to do with them. There are two layers to keep apart. The first is what the values *mean* (the statistical type), and the second is how the computer *stores* them (the storage type).

**What the values mean.** The classical scheme sorts a column by the operations that make sense on it:

+------------------+------------------------+------------------------+----------------------------+----------------+
| Type             | Subtype                | Example                | What makes sense           | In `covid.csv` |
+:=================+:=======================+:=======================+:===========================+:===============+
| **Categorical**  | **nominal**: which     | state, blood type,     | equal or not equal;        | `state`,       |
| (a fixed set of  | group?                 | country                | counting; no order         | `county`       |
| levels)          +------------------------+------------------------+----------------------------+----------------+
|                  | **ordinal**: which     | grade (A, B, C), shirt | order (<, >), but the gaps | none           |
|                  | group, in a *ranked*   | size (S, M, L),        | between levels are not     |                |
|                  | order?                 | "disagree / neutral /  | meaningful                 |                |
|                  |                        | agree"                 |                            |                |
+------------------+------------------------+------------------------+----------------------------+----------------+
| **Numeric**      | **interval**: how far  | temperature in         | differences (30°C is 10°   | `date`         |
| (arithmetic      | apart?                 | Celsius, a calendar    | warmer than 20°C), but no  |                |
| makes sense, at  |                        | date                   | ratios: the zero is        |                |
| least in part)   |                        |                        | arbitrary, so 30°C is not  |                |
|                  |                        |                        | "1.5 times as hot" as 20°C |                |
|                  +------------------------+------------------------+----------------------------+----------------+
|                  | **ratio, continuous**: | height, weight,        | everything: differences    | none           |
|                  | how much?              | income, time spent,    | *and* ratios, because zero |                |
|                  |                        | temperature in Kelvin  | means "none" (20 kg is     |                |
|                  |                        |                        | twice 10 kg)               |                |
|                  +------------------------+------------------------+----------------------------+----------------+
|                  | **ratio, discrete**:   | number of cases,       | everything a ratio allows, | `cases`,       |
|                  | how many whole things? | children in a family,  | but the values are only    | `deaths`       |
|                  | (a **count**)          | clicks on a page       | the whole numbers 0, 1, 2, |                |
|                  |                        |                        | ... (never 1.5)            |                |
+------------------+------------------------+------------------------+----------------------------+----------------+
| **Text /**       |                        | a tweet, an address, a | search and parse it; not a | none           |
| **character**    |                        | comment                | categorical until you      |                |
| (free text):     |                        |                        | extract the L categories   |                |
| what was         |                        |                        |                            |                |
| written?         |                        |                        |                            |                |
+------------------+------------------------+------------------------+----------------------------+----------------+

: The statistical types. A **categorical** column has a fixed set of levels (nominal or ordinal), and a **numeric** column holds numbers (interval or ratio). A count is a ratio that is **discrete** (only whole numbers); the other numeric subtypes are **continuous**.

A few places where this is not obvious:

* **A code that looks like a number is nominal.** `fips` is made of digits, but adding two FIPS codes or taking their mean is meaningless. It is a label for a county, so it should be stored as text. (In the next unit we will watch a program silently turn the code `06059` into `6059`.)
* **A count and a measurement are both ratios, but they behave differently.** `cases` can be 0, 1, 2, but never 1.5, so it is a discrete count. A measured quantity such as height is continuous. Both have a true zero, but you use different models for them later in the course, and they are stored differently (integer versus decimal, see below).
* **A yes/no column is a special case**, called binary. It is nominal with exactly two levels (stored as `true` / `false`).
* **Ordinal data is the one most often mishandled.** If you store grades A, B, C as 1, 2, 3, a program will happily average them, and it will treat the step from A to B as the same size as the step from B to C. Keep the order, but do not do arithmetic on it.
* **Missing values are part of the type.** In `covid.csv`, 8,266 rows have no `fips` (mostly the county `Unknown`, plus a few cities) and 18,761 rows have no `deaths`. A column of integers cannot hold "missing" in many programs, so they silently turn the whole column into decimals: `pandas` read `deaths` as `float64` for this reason.

**How the values are stored.** The computer needs a concrete representation for each statistical type. These are the storage types you will meet in R and `pandas`:

+----------------------+-----------------------+-----------------------+----------------------+
| Statistical type     | Typical storage type  | R                     | `pandas`             |
+:=====================+:======================+:======================+:=====================+
| nominal              | text, or a dictionary | `character`, `factor` | `object` / `string`, |
|                      | of levels             |                       | `category`           |
+----------------------+-----------------------+-----------------------+----------------------+
| ordinal              | the same, with the    | `ordered` factor      | ordered `category`   |
|                      | level order recorded  |                       |                      |
+----------------------+-----------------------+-----------------------+----------------------+
| interval or ratio, a | decimal ("floating    | `numeric`             | `float64`            |
| measurement          | point")               |                       |                      |
| (Celsius, height,    |                       |                       |                      |
| income)              |                       |                       |                      |
+----------------------+-----------------------+-----------------------+----------------------+
| count                | integer               | `integer`             | `int64`              |
+----------------------+-----------------------+-----------------------+----------------------+
| date or time         | a date or a timestamp | `Date`, `POSIXct`     | `datetime64`         |
+----------------------+-----------------------+-----------------------+----------------------+
| binary               | boolean               | `logical`             | `bool`               |
+----------------------+-----------------------+-----------------------+----------------------+
| character (free      | text                  | `character`           | `object` / `string`  |
| text)                |                       |                       |                      |
+----------------------+-----------------------+-----------------------+----------------------+

: The storage types. The names differ between R and Python, but the ideas are the same. The interval and ratio rows are one row, on purpose.

Notice that programs do not distinguish interval from ratio: both are stored as decimals, and the difference exists only in what you may sensibly compute with them (a ratio of two Celsius temperatures is a number, but a meaningless one). What programs *do* distinguish is integer from decimal (`integer` versus `numeric` in R, `int64` versus `float64` in `pandas`), which is why counts get their own row. A date is stored as a number of days since a fixed starting day, with a label that says to show it as a date.

A CSV stores all of these as text and leaves every program to guess the storage type, which is what goes wrong with `fips` in the next unit. A better file format would store the type with the data, so that a `date` stays a date, `cases` stays an integer and `fips` stays text. For a nominal column such as `state`, with 55 distinct values repeated on 885,000 rows, it could store the small list of levels once and then a short code per row (**dictionary encoding**), which also makes the column small. The same idea in R is a `factor` and in `pandas` is a `category`.

# A better data format than CSV?

The CSV is the universal format for tabular data, and you will receive data in it for the rest of your career. But a CSV is just the bare table: no column types, nothing about what is inside, and no way to read part of it without reading all of it. Before we go all the way to a database, there is a middle step that is still just a file you can copy, send to others and commit in your repo: **Parquet**.

Think of Parquet as **annotated tabular data**. It stores the same table as the CSV, plus notes about the table, written into the file itself: the name and type of every column, how each column was compressed, and a summary (the smallest and largest value) of every block of rows. Those annotations are what make it

* **fast to read**: a program knows the types in advance, so it does not parse and guess, and it can read just the columns it needs, and
* **fast to query**: the summaries let a program skip the blocks that cannot contain the answer without even reading them.

This unit motivates the annotated format, converts `covid.csv`, and then shows what happens when the data is really large: it keeps working, in R and in Python, when the CSV would not even fit in memory.

## What is wrong with a CSV?

Three complaints that need no database at all:

1. **It is big.** Text spends one byte per digit and writes `Texas` out again on 67,002 rows. Our `covid.csv` is 35 MB, and `gzip` can squeeze it to 9 MB, but then every tool must unpack it first.
2. **It has no types.** A CSV does not know that `date` is a date, that `cases` is an integer, or that `fips` is a *code* and not a number. Every program guesses on every read. Guess `fips` is an integer and the code `06059` (Orange County, California) silently becomes `6059`. Compare what the two languages guess on the same file:

```bash
Rscript -e 'library(data.table); str(fread("covid.csv", nrows = 1000))'     # fips: int
python3 -c 'import pandas as pd; print(pd.read_csv("covid.csv", nrows=1000).dtypes)'   # fips: float64 (the column has missing values)
```

3. **You must read everything to get anything.** A CSV is stored row by row, so a question about two columns still reads (and parses) all six. The lectures' `cut -d, -f3` has to scan every byte of every line to find the third comma.

Parquet stores the column types (text, integers, decimals, dates and timestamps, true/false, and a dictionary form for columns with few distinct values) in the file itself, so the guessing is gone.

What we want is the same table with annotations: a file that is **smaller**, **typed**, and lets us **read only the columns we need**. That is Parquet.

## A short history

Parquet is not old, and it came out of a specific problem: companies with petabytes of logs on Hadoop clusters whose queries were slow because they read row after row of text.

+-----------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|      Year | What happened                                                                  |
+==========:+:===============================================================================+
|      2010 | Google publishes the **Dremel** paper: how to store even nested records *by    |
|           | column*, so a query touches only the columns it names. Google used it          |
|           | internally for web-scale analytics (it later became BigQuery).                 |
+-----------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|      2013 | **Twitter** and **Cloudera** (whose Impala engine needed a fast file format)   |
|           | build an open-source version of Dremel's storage ideas and call it Parquet.    |
|           | About the same time, Hive's **ORC** format appears with the same idea.         |
+-----------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|      2015 | Parquet becomes a top-level project of the Apache Software Foundation, the     |
|           | home of Hadoop and Spark.                                                      |
+-----------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|      2016 | **Apache Arrow**, started by Wes McKinney (the author of `pandas`), defines    |
|           | the same columnar layout *in memory*. Parquet on disk and Arrow in memory fit  |
|           | together, which is why Python and R can read Parquet so quickly.               |
+-----------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|      2017 | `pandas` gets `read_parquet` and `to_parquet`, and R gets the `arrow` package. |
|           | Parquet leaves the Hadoop world.                                               |
+-----------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| 2018-2019 | **Iceberg** (from Netflix) and **Delta Lake** (from Databricks) appear: table  |
|           | formats that add transactions and "undo" on top of folders of Parquet files.   |
|           | **DuckDB**, a database that queries a Parquet file directly, appears.          |
+-----------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

: Dates are from my memory of the projects' histories; check the Apache Parquet site before quoting one.

## How popular is it?

There is no number like the "share of developers" we quoted for `git`, because nobody surveys file formats. What we can say is where it shows up, and that is nearly everywhere in data engineering:

* **Engines read and write it.** Spark writes Parquet by default, and Snowflake, BigQuery, AWS Athena and DuckDB all load, export or query it directly.
* **Table formats are built on it.** Delta Lake and Iceberg, the standard ways of organizing a company's folders of files into tables, store their data *as Parquet files* plus a layer of bookkeeping.
* **Both our languages support it.** `pandas`, `polars`, and R's `arrow` read and write it, so a Parquet file made in Python opens in R unchanged. That makes it the format of choice for *handing data between tools*, unlike a `.pkl` or `.rds`.
* **Public data is published in it**, for example many datasets on the Hugging Face hub and large open datasets on cloud storage.

It has rivals: **ORC** (the same idea, mostly in the Hive world), **Avro** (row-based, popular for streams of events), and newer formats still being tested. But if you join a data team and ask "what format is the data in?", the most likely answer today is "Parquet".

## Converting `covid.csv`

First, say what each column *is*. In Python, `dtype` and `parse_dates` do it; then `to_parquet` writes the file (it needs the `pyarrow` package):

```python
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("covid.csv", dtype={"fips": str}, parse_dates=["date"])   # fips is a code (text), date is a date
print(df.dtypes)
df.to_parquet("covid.parquet", compression="zstd")
```

In R, the `arrow` package does the same. `schema(fips = string())` overrides the guess for just that column:

```r
library(arrow)
df <- read_csv_arrow("covid.csv", col_types = schema(fips = string()))
write_parquet(df, "covid.parquet", compression = "zstd")
```

Now compare the files:

```bash
ls -alh covid.csv covid.parquet     # 35M versus 3.4M
file covid.parquet                  # Apache Parquet
gzip -k covid.csv; ls -alh covid.csv.gz; rm covid.csv.gz     # 8.9M: the CSV zipped
head -c 4 covid.parquet; echo; tail -c 4 covid.parquet       # PAR1 at both ends: the "magic bytes"
```

The Parquet file is about **10 times smaller** than the CSV, and even smaller than the gzipped CSV, **and** it can be read directly. Reading it back keeps the types, so `date` is still a date and `fips` is still the text `"06059"` without anybody guessing:

```python
pd.read_parquet("covid.parquet").dtypes
```

And you can ask for only the columns you want:

```python
pd.read_parquet("covid.parquet", columns=["state", "cases"])   # reads two of the six columns
```

Here are our timings in `pandas` on this file (one run on one machine; yours will differ but the ranking should not):

+-------------------------------+---------+---------+
| Task                          | CSV     | Parquet |
+:==============================+========:+========:+
| File size                     | 35.9 MB | 3.4 MB  |
+-------------------------------+---------+---------+
| Read the whole table          | 0.65 s  | 0.03 s  |
+-------------------------------+---------+---------+
| Read only `state` and `cases` | 0.31 s  | 0.02 s  |
+-------------------------------+---------+---------+

Notice that the CSV cannot make the two-column read much faster (`usecols` still has to scan every line), while Parquet gets faster because it never touches the other columns.

Be fair to the CSV, though: those timings are for `pandas`, whose CSV reader is slow. R's `data.table::fread` is one of the fastest CSV readers there is, and on this 35 MB file it loads the whole table in 0.10 s, about as fast as reading the Parquet file (0.15 s into a `data.table`). The columns-only read is where Parquet already wins (0.025 s versus 0.05 s for `fread` with `select=`). At 35 MB nobody should care about any of this. The real difference shows up when the file is much bigger, and that is the section after next.

## Why is it small and fast?

Three ideas, none of them magic:

* **Columns, not rows.** The values of one column are stored together. `state` becomes a long run of the same few dozen words, which compresses extremely well; `cases` is a run of integers. Mixing text and numbers in every line, as a CSV does, spoils both.
* **Types and encodings.** An integer is stored as an integer, not as characters. A column with few distinct values (the 55 states) is stored as a small dictionary plus a list of codes (**dictionary encoding**).
* **A footer of summary statistics.** At the end of the file, Parquet stores the min and max of every column for every block of rows (a **row group**). A query for `cases > 700000` can skip every block whose maximum is lower without reading it. You can see these:

```python
import pyarrow.parquet as pq
pf = pq.ParquetFile("covid.parquet")
print(pf.schema_arrow)                          # names and types
print(pf.metadata.row_group(0).column(4))       # min, max, compression of the cases column
```

## When the data is really large

Everything above fits in memory on any laptop. So let us make a dataset that is 50 times bigger: `covid.csv` stacked 50 times, with a `copy` column saying which copy a row came from. That is 44 million rows. (The numbers are copies of each other, so this is a toy dataset, but the size and the shape are real.) The script is in `lectures/scripts/lec03/` and writes the data twice: once as a single big CSV, and once as a **folder of Parquet files**, one file per copy:

```bash
python3 ../../lectures/scripts/lec03/make_covid_big.py covid.csv 50 --csv   # about 80 seconds
ls -alh covid_big.csv        # 1.8G
du -sh covid_big             # 163M: 50 Parquet files
ls covid_big | head -3       # copy=0  copy=1  copy=10
ls covid_big/copy=0          # part-0.parquet
```

The folder names `copy=0`, `copy=1`, ... follow a convention called **hive partitioning**: the name of a folder holds the value of a column, so the column does not have to be stored inside the files. The question for both versions: *what is the total of `cases` in Texas, separately for every copy?*

**The CSV way:** load everything, then ask. In R and in Python:

```r
library(data.table)
d <- fread("covid_big.csv")                                        # all 44M rows into memory
d[state == "Texas", .(cases = sum(cases)), by = copy]
```

```python
import pandas as pd
d = pd.read_csv("covid_big.csv", dtype={"fips": str})              # all 44M rows into memory
d[d.state == "Texas"].groupby("copy").cases.sum()
```

**The Parquet way:** point at the folder and ask. Nothing is loaded up front. The program works out which parts of which files it needs, reads only those, and returns just the small answer:

```r
library(arrow); library(dplyr)
open_dataset("covid_big") |>                                       # a lazy handle on the folder
  filter(state == "Texas") |>
  group_by(copy) |>
  summarise(cases = sum(cases)) |>
  collect()                                                        # now it runs, and returns 50 rows
```

```python
import pyarrow.dataset as ds, pyarrow.compute as pc
d = ds.dataset("covid_big", format="parquet", partitioning="hive")
d.to_table(columns=["copy", "cases"], filter=pc.field("state") == "Texas") \
 .group_by("copy").aggregate([("cases", "sum")])
```

Time each one, and ask Linux for the most memory it used (the line `Maximum resident set size`):

```bash
/usr/bin/time -v Rscript query.R 2> time.txt; grep "Maximum resident" time.txt
```

Our results (one run on a 12-core machine with 41 GB of memory; yours will differ but the ranking should not):

+------------------------+--------------------------------+--------------------------------+
|                        | CSV: load everything, then ask | Parquet: ask the folder        |
+:=======================+===============================:+===============================:+
| File size on disk      | 1.8 GB                         | 163 MB                         |
+------------------------+--------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| R: time                | 29 s (`fread`)                 | 2.7 s (`arrow`)                |
+------------------------+--------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| R: peak memory         | 3.7 GB                         | 0.6 GB                         |
+------------------------+--------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| Python: time           | 113 s (`pandas`)               | 1.9 s (`pyarrow`)              |
+------------------------+--------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| Python: peak memory    | 6.5 GB                         | 0.6 GB                         |
+------------------------+--------------------------------+--------------------------------+

Read the memory rows carefully. The CSV versions need several gigabytes *because they load all the data first*, and that is the number that decides whether your laptop can do the job at all. On a laptop with 8 GB of memory and a file ten times this size, `fread` and `pandas` simply fail with "out of memory". The Parquet versions stay at about 0.6 GB, because they stream through the files a piece at a time and keep only the running totals. The same code would work on a 500 GB folder. (The 163 MB is flattering: the 50 copies are identical, which compresses much better than real data does. The memory and the speed advantage are the real result.)

How can it be this much faster? The annotations again:

* It read **3 of the 7 columns** (`state`, `cases`, `copy`) and never touched the others.
* It used the **row-group statistics** to skip blocks that cannot contain Texas.
* It processed **one file at a time**, so memory never held the whole dataset.
* And with the folder names it can skip files entirely. Ask only about the first five copies, and it opens only five folders (**partition pruning**). That took 0.34 s in R and 0.15 s in Python on our machine:

```r
open_dataset("covid_big") |> filter(state == "Texas", copy < 5) |> group_by(copy) |> summarise(cases = sum(cases)) |> collect()
```

The same folder can be asked with SQL by DuckDB, a database that runs on Parquet files and is available in both R and Python. In R, the `duckdb` package gave the same answer in 1.3 s:

```r
con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT copy, sum(cases) AS cases
                      FROM read_parquet('covid_big/*/*.parquet', hive_partitioning = true)
                      WHERE state = 'Texas' GROUP BY copy")
```

### Can't `awk` do this in constant memory?

Yes, and that is a fair objection, because a streaming tool never loads the data. Count the rows in each state, first with `awk` on the CSV and then with `arrow` on the Parquet folder:

```bash
awk -F, 'NR>1 {n[$3]++} END {for (s in n) print s "," n[s]}' covid_big.csv | sort -t, -k2,2nr | head -n 3
```

```r
open_dataset("covid_big") |> count(state) |> arrange(desc(n)) |> collect()
```

Both give the same answer (Texas 3,350,100, Georgia 2,260,450, Virginia 1,844,300). We also timed a second question with each tool, the total of Texas `cases` for each `copy`:

+--------------------------------------+---------------------+-----------------------+
|                                      | `awk` on the CSV    | `arrow` on Parquet    |
+:=====================================+====================:+======================:+
| Rows per state: time                 | 144 s               | 2.8 s                 |
+--------------------------------------+---------------------+-----------------------+
| Texas cases per copy: time           | 156 s               | 2.5 s                 |
+--------------------------------------+---------------------+-----------------------+
| Peak memory (rows per state)         | 4.6 MB              | 405 MB                |
+--------------------------------------+---------------------+-----------------------+

: One run, one machine. `awk` uses one core, `arrow` uses all twelve.

On memory, `awk` wins by a factor of nearly a hundred: 4.6 MB, because it keeps only a counter for each of the 55 states. The price is **time**. `awk` has to read and split every one of the 1.8 GB for *every* question, so each question costs about two and a half minutes, and ten questions cost half an hour. `arrow` answered in under three seconds, because the first question needed only the `state` column (one of seven) and it spread the work over all the cores. Converting the CSV to Parquet costs one pass, once, and then every later question is cheap.

Streaming also has limits that Parquet does not. `awk` stays at constant memory only when the number of groups is small: a table of 44 million different keys would not fit in a hash map. A median needs all the values, a sort needs temporary files, and a join needs one of the two tables in memory. And as the `cut` example earlier showed, it breaks on a CSV with quoted fields (note that we had to turn quoting off to write `covid_big.csv`, or `awk` would see `"Texas"` with the quotes).

So the honest rule is: for a single question about a file you will read once, `awk` on the CSV is fine and Parquet does not help. Parquet pays off when you will ask **many** questions about the **same** large table, and when each question touches only some of its columns.

Clean up the big files when you are done, since they take about 2 GB: `rm -r covid_big covid_big.csv`.

## What it cannot do

* **It is binary.** `head`, `grep`, `cut` and `awk` show gibberish. You need a program that understands Parquet, which is why the shell tools from lectures 1 and 2 are for the *before* step and Parquet is for the *after*.
* **It is write-once.** You cannot change one value in place or append a row to the file; you rewrite it. (Delta Lake and Iceberg exist to hide this.)
* **It is still just a file.** It has no indexes, no users, and nothing stops two programs from writing at once. For that you need a database, which is next.

## Which format when?
